1) Odontogenic buccal-space infection/abscess (occult periapical tooth source) — most likely given localized mid‑cheek pain and tenderness despite a normal panoramic film (small periapical lesions or buccal cortical involvement can be missed on OPG). Next confirmatory steps: focused dental exam and percussion of UL teeth, periapical radiographs of the left maxillary premolars/molars and/or dental CBCT; intraoral inspection for sinus tract.

2) Infected epidermal/epidermoid or sebaceous inclusion cyst (cutis/subcutis) — fits a chronic, localized, tender buccal swelling that can persist for months and become intermittently painful when infected. Next steps: inspect skin surface, high‑resolution soft‑tissue ultrasound to look for a cystic lesion, consider incision/drainage ± culture if fluctuant.

3) Minor salivary gland lesion (mucocele/retention cyst or chronic minor-salivary-gland sialadenitis) — minor salivary glands on the buccal mucosa can produce persistent swelling; mucoceles are usually fluctuant but can be painful if inflamed. Next steps: careful intraoral exam, ultrasound, ENT/dentist evaluation and possible excisional biopsy.

4) Minor salivary gland neoplasm (e.g., pleomorphic adenoma of a buccal minor gland) — presents as a chronic, often slowly enlarging mass; pain is less common but possible if secondarily inflamed. Next steps: ultrasound, MRI if solid, and fine‑needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) or excisional biopsy for tissue diagnosis.

5) Chronic lymphadenitis (including atypical mycobacterial/TB) or nodal/metastatic disease (lymphoma, metastasis) — chronicity and localized swelling could represent an involved node or soft‑tissue lymphoid process. Next steps: neck and intraoral exam, ultrasound with FNAC of the lesion, CBC, ESR/CRP, chest X‑ray and TB testing as indicated.

Highest‑priority immediate actions I recommend: focused intraoral and skin inspection of the left buccal area, soft‑tissue ultrasound of the cheek, targeted periapical dental radiographs/CBCT of left maxillary teeth, and consider FNAC if ultrasound shows a solid lesion. These will distinguish odontogenic vs cutaneous vs salivary vs nodal causes and guide definitive management.
